section: Why Not Just Use PubMed Alerts?
text:
Why Not Just Use PubMed Alerts?
PubMed alerts are a reasonable starting point, but they have a key limitation: they give you a flat, unsorted list. If you set up an alert for “inflammatory bowel disease,” every matching paper arrives in the same inbox pile - therapeutics next to epidemiology next to basic science - and you still have to read through everything to find what’s relevant to your work.
IBD LitMonitor takes a different approach. Instead of delivering a raw feed, it organizes papers into sub-fields so you can go straight to the topic area you care about and skip the rest. Each category is collapsible, so browsing the day’s literature takes minutes rather than a lengthy inbox triage.

Daily process:

Search PubMed across category-specific query groups

Sort by publication date (newest first within each category)
Publish updated website, RSS feed, and per-category RSS feeds

Papers by Category






NoteHow to Read This Report



Coverage: PubMed queries across a broad set of IBD topic groups, deduplicated - each paper appears exactly once in the most specific matching category.
Categorisation: Automatic and imperfect - a paper found by multiple queries is assigned to the most specific one (e.g. a vedolizumab trial in children goes to Pediatric IBD). For keyword search across all categories or papers from the past 30 days, use the Interactive Dashboard.
Study design badges RCT Meta-analysis Review are shown only when PubMed has explicitly assigned a publication type. Papers published within the last 1-2 weeks often don’t have a badge yet.
★ Flagship journals: Papers from Gut, Gastroenterology, Lancet, NEJM, JCC, and other leading GI journals are marked ★.
Spotted something wrong or have a suggestion?  Send feedback →


Click a category to expand. Click a paper title to read its abstract.


Microbiome & Immunology  (16 papers)



Functionally declining microbiota in chronic disease: beyond taxonomic loss.Review★  Gut microbes  |  2026-10-15



Microbiota deterioration in modern human populations has been linked to chronic disease, and taxonomic profiling is increasingly used to understand, diagnose, and guide treatment. Yet such profiles do not fully capture disease-relevant microbiota states. I propose functional decline within retained taxa as a distinct axis of microbiota deterioration, complementary to taxonomic loss. Modern environmental pressures can drive not only taxonomic loss but also directional selection toward variants or lineages with reduced host-beneficial function or increased harmful activity. Two mechanistically characterized systems from studies by my group illustrate this process: antibiotic-selected Akkermansia variants with diminished metabolic benefits, and Faecalibacterium pathobionts that promote disease when dominant over beneficial strains, with supporting evidence from atopic dermatitis and pediatric inflammatory bowel disease. Evidence from additional gut taxa suggests that this pattern may extend beyond these two examples. By integrating this hidden axis of functional decline with the well-established axis of taxonomic loss, the proposed two-axis framework could help clarify inconsistent microbiota-disease associations and guide strain-resolved, function-first approaches to microbiota analysis and intervention.


Kim HS


DOI: 10.1080/19490976.2026.2748134  |  View on PubMed →





Enteric ChAT-Expressing Neurons Mediate the Protective Effect of Lactobacillus plantarum in Inflammatory Bowel Disease.★  Advanced science (Weinheim, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany)  |  2026-10-14



The gut microbiota plays a crucial role in inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), yet how specific microbial components influence disease progression remains incompletely understood. Our study reveals that decreased abundance of Lactobacillus species correlates with ulcerative colitis severity in patients. Among tested strains, L. plantarum A736, isolated from traditional fermented foods, demonstrated protective effects in ameliorating dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis in a mouse model. Strikingly, multi-omics analysis revealed that L. plantarum A736 uniquely enhances choline acetyltransferase-expressing (ChAT+) neurons in the enteric nervous system and elevates acetylcholine (ACh) levels. Further analysis identified that L. plantarum A736 metabolizes tryptophan to produce indole-3-lactic acid (ILA), and supplementation with ILA significantly mimics this strain’s anti-inflammatory effects by restoring ChAT+ neurons and cholinergic signaling. Crucially, selective ablation of colonic ChAT+ neurons abolished the protective effect of both L. plantarum A736 and ILA, establishing their essential role in mediating these effects. These findings demonstrate that microbial metabolites can modulate enteric neuronal circuits to regulate gut immunity. The identified ILA-ChAT+ neuron axis represents a novel neuro-immune pathway that could be targeted for IBD treatment.


Xia B, Sun Y, Wang J, Liu Y, Wang L, Jiang S, Bai G, Zhang R, Zhang Y, Kou R


DOI: 10.1002/advs.77455  |  View on PubMed →





Sargassum soluble dietary fiber alleviates oxidative stress and gut microbiota dysbiosis to prevent inflammatory bowel disease in C57BL/6 mice.  Journal of the science of food and agriculture  |  2026-10-14



Fermentation may enhance the bioactivity of Sargassum soluble dietary fiber (SDF). This study investigates the preventive effects of Bifidobacterium longum fermented Sargassum SDF (BL-SDF) against oxidative stress and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). In vitro, the BL-SDF significantly reduced nitric oxide (NO) production by 16.98-23.04% and reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation by 65.30-81.28% in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages, increased superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT) activities, decreased malondialdehyde (MDA), and suppressed prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β). In dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced C57BL/6 mice, pre-administration of BL-SDF alleviated weight loss and colonic damage, enhanced antioxidant enzymes activities (SOD, CAT, and glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px)), and reduced MDA and NO levels in the colon. Additionally, 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) sequencing analysis further indicated enrichment of Incertae_Sedis group, Faecalibaculum, and Roseburia, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) revealed elevation of acetic acid, propionic acid, butyric acid, and valeric acid (P < 0.05). Concurrently, BL-SDF significantly reduced the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines including TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and interleukin-23 (IL-23). BL-SDF alleviates intestinal inflammation by enhancing antioxidant activities and modulating gut microbiota, suggesting that fermented Sargassum SDF may serve as a dietary strategy for preventing inflammatory bowel disease. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.


Cai H, Li E, Wang Z, Li R, Zhao Q, Song B, Liu X, Huang R, Xu B, Liu S


DOI: 10.1002/jsfa.71167  |  View on PubMed →





Mediterranean diet, gut microbiota, and intestinal barrier integrity: implications for digestive and systemic health.Review  Antonie van Leeuwenhoek  |  2026-10-13



The Mediterranean diet has gained increasing attention for its effects on gut microbiota, microbial metabolism, intestinal barrier function, and related clinical outcomes. This narrative review critically synthesizes evidence from 51 publications identified through structured searches of PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar, including human intervention studies, observational studies, systematic and narrative reviews, and selected preclinical studies. The available evidence suggests that the MD can influence microbial composition and function, although taxonomic responses vary considerably between populations and study designs. More consistent findings involve microbial metabolic activity, particularly short-chain fatty acid production, bile acid remodeling, and polyphenol-derived metabolites. These changes may contribute to intestinal barrier regulation, mucosal homeostasis, and immune modulation. Human intervention studies provide supportive evidence in inflammatory bowel disease, functional gastrointestinal disorders, obesity, metabolic syndrome, and related conditions, while evidence for neurological, autoimmune, and cancer-related outcomes remains more limited and is often observational or mechanistic. Direct evidence for improved intestinal barrier function is still less extensive than indirect evidence based on inflammatory markers, microbial metabolites, and permeability-related measures. Differences in microbiome methodology, baseline diet, disease status, geographic background, and intervention duration contribute to variability across studies. The MD therefore represents a promising dietary framework for modulating gut microbial function and intestinal homeostasis, but further long-term and mechanistically integrated human studies are needed to define causal pathways and identify individuals most likely to benefit.


Perets TT


DOI: 10.1007/s10482-026-02436-1  |  View on PubMed →





B cells regulate T cell transfer colitis by partially reconstituting luminal IgA and modulating the colonic microbiota.★  Inflammatory bowel diseases  |  2026-10-12



Loss of immune tolerance to commensal microbial antigens is a central driver of inflammatory bowel disease. While regulatory T cells are well recognized in maintaining intestinal homeostasis, the contribution of B cells-particularly IgA-secreting cells-remains incompletely defined. In the T cell transfer colitis model, cotransfer of splenic B cells attenuates disease, an effect largely attributed to IL-10-producing regulatory B cells (Bregs). However, alternative B cell-dependent mechanisms have not been fully explored. Here, we investigated whether splenic B cells regulate T cell transfer colitis through IgA-dependent mechanisms independent of Breg-associated cytokines. We show that splenic B cells from wild-type C57BL/6 (B6) mice reconstitute bone marrow and peripheral B cell compartments in RAG1⁻/⁻ recipients, undergo class switching, migrate to the colonic lamina propria as sIgA⁺ B lineage cells, and partially restore luminal secretory IgA. B cell cotransfer significantly attenuated clinical and histological colitis without increased expression of canonical Breg-associated cytokines, including interleukin-10, transforming growth factor β, and interleukin-35 subunits. In contrast, splenic B cells from IgA-deficient mice failed to attenuate colitis despite comparable peripheral B cell reconstitution. Restoration of secretory IgA was associated with increased bacterial IgA coating, reduced fecal bacterial burden, and remodeling of the colonic microbiota, including enrichment of beneficial commensal taxa. Importantly, because IgA-deficient B cells failed to attenuate colitis despite comparable peripheral B cell reconstitution, these findings support an important role for IgA in mediating the protective effect of B cell transfer. Collectively, these findings identify IgA-mediated modulation of the microbiota as an alternate mechanism by which B cells attenuate T cell transfer colitis, highlighting a Breg-independent regulatory pathway with potential relevance to inflammatory bowel disease pathogenesis.


Urrete J, Kim M, Chilukuri A, Kaur P, Shen Z, Holton M, Jedlicka P, Urtecho G, Bamias G, Rivera-Nieves J


DOI: 10.1093/ibd/izag198  |  View on PubMed →





β-Glucan-based oral nano/micro delivery systems: harnessing dual immunomodulatory and microbiota-modulating properties for targeted therapy of cancer and inflammatory bowel disease.Review  Nanoscale  |  2026-10-12



The efficacy of oral drug delivery is often constrained by gastrointestinal physiological barriers and the hepatic first-pass effect, while conventional oral formulations lack the capability of targeted release at intestinal lesions, creating an urgent need for innovative functional delivery carriers. β-Glucan, an abundant natural polysaccharide, holds great potential for constructing intelligent oral nano/micro delivery systems, owing to its resistance to human digestive enzymes and its inherent dual immunomodulatory and microbiota-regulating properties. This carrier not only serves as an ideal protective vehicle but also bypasses the first-pass effect via M-cell-mediated lymphatic targeting and achieves site-specific drug release at pathological sites through its susceptibility to colonic microbiota enzymatic degradation. This review emphasizes the structural diversity, structure-activity relationships, and combined immunomodulatory/microbiota-modulating functions of β-glucan. It further explains how M-cell targeting and microbiota responsiveness are integrated to overcome gastrointestinal barriers for precise intestinal and systemic delivery. Recent advances in β-glucan-based nano/micro delivery systems for the treatment of cancer and inflammatory bowel disease are also highlighted. Finally, current challenges and future directions for β-glucan-based oral nano/micro delivery systems are outlined. In summary, the unique properties of β-glucan offer exciting new opportunities for targeted oral drug delivery.


Fu Y, Cao C, Jiao Y, Cao Y, Hao H, Cui X, Gao D, Gao Y, Zhang Q, Liu Y


DOI: 10.1039/d6nr02259f  |  View on PubMed →





Morganella morganii-derived histamine impairs intestinal barrier function via HRH4 and aggravates colitis.★  Inflammatory bowel diseases  |  2026-10-09



Pro-inflammatory dietary patterns are associated with an increased risk of Crohn’s disease (CD) and shifts in the gut microbiota. Our previous multi-omics analysis had identified the enrichment of Morganella morganii (M. morganii) in both patients with CD and individuals consuming pro-inflammatory diets. In this study, we aimed to investigate the role and potential mechanisms by which M. morganii contributes to intestinal inflammation. Using murine models of colitis, mouse colon organoids, and epithelial cell systems, combined with metabolomic profiling and pharmacological interventions, we investigated the effects of M. morganii and its secreted metabolites on tight junction integrity and intestinal permeability. M. morganii aggravated colitis severity and induced a remarkable increase in intestinal permeability with disruption of tight junction architecture, including reduced occludin and zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) expression and ultrastructural damage. These effects were predominantly mediated by the secreted low-molecular-weight metabolites rather than by bacterial invasion. Metabolomic analysis of the <3-kDa fraction of M. morganii culture supernatant identified histamine as a key bioactive molecule. Histamine recapitulated barrier disruption and colitis exacerbation in vivo. Pharmacological studies suggested that histamine-induced injury is mediated mainly through the histamine receptor H4 (HRH4) and that the inhibition of histamine synthesis significantly restored barrier integrity and alleviated colitis. These findings suggest a previously unrecognized pathway in which the diet-responsive pathobiont M. morganii may impair epithelial barrier integrity through histamine-HRH4 signaling. Targeting histamine synthesis and HRH4 may offer a potential therapeutic avenue worth further investigation.


Yi Y, Feng R, Wu X, Zhu X, Xiang L, Zheng K, Xu S, Lai W, Zhu Y, Chen M

Context-dependent roles of ketone metabolism in intestinal inflammation.Review  Trends in immunology  |  2026-10-08



Ketone metabolism is traditionally viewed as an alternative metabolic pathway providing energy during carbohydrate deprivation through the production and utilization of ketone bodies. Ketone bodies also function as signaling molecules regulating immune and metabolic processes. Accumulating evidence shows that ketone metabolism influences diverse diseases and immune responses, including inflammation, autoimmunity, and infection. Recently, ketone metabolism has been associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a chronic inflammatory disorder of the intestine, although reported effects are heterogeneous and context-dependent. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on ketone metabolism in IBD and intestinal inflammation, highlighting its roles in barrier integrity, immune regulation, and microbiota interactions. We also discuss potential mechanisms underlying divergent outcomes and outline key questions for future research.


Dong W, Yan C, Korwin-Mihavics B, Alexander M


DOI: 10.1016/j.it.2026.09.005  |  View on PubMed →





Tegoprazan regulates gut microbiota structure in Helicobacter pylori-induced ulcerative colitis mice.  Folia microbiologica  |  2026-10-08



Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection promotes pathogenesis of ulcerative colitis (UC). Tegoprazan, as the firs-line therapy for H. pylori eradication, alleviates inflammatory bowel disease. This study aimed to investigate the effects of Tegoprazan on UC. Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection was performed to establish a mouse UC model. Histological analysis was conducted using HE staining and Alcian blue-periodic acid Schiff staining. Gene expression was detected using Western blot and RT-qPCR. Cytokine levels were analyzed using ELISA. Cell apoptosis was analyzed using TUNEL. Gut microbiota structure was analyzed using 16s rRNA sequencing. Tegoprazan alleviated H. pylori infection-induced the destruction of the crypt structure and intestinal barrier structure. Moreover, Tegoprazan inhibited the inflammatory response and the death of goblet cells. Moreover, gut microbiota achieved a new equilibrium state. Teg mediated the eradication of H. pylori and the release of short-chain fatty acids. Taken together, Tegoprazan protects against the progression of UC through regulating gut microbiota and regulating fatty acid metabolism, improving intestinal mucosal barrier integrity. Clinical trial: not applicable.


Tang A, Zhao M, Long Y, Cai Y


DOI: 10.1007/s12223-026-01603-1  |  View on PubMed →





Anemoside B4 from Pulsatilla chinensis Ameliorates Ulcerative Colitis by Inhibiting Inflammatory Responses via the Modulation of the Gut Microbiota-Immune Interplay.  The American journal of Chinese medicine  |  2026-10-08



We previously demonstrated that anemoside B4 (AB4) exerts a beneficial effect in a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced murine model of ulcerative colitis (UC). In this study, we further explored the mechanism of AB4 against UC from the perspective of gut microbiota-immune interplay. The gut microbiota was depleted in two DSS-induced colitis models to investigate the modulatory effects of the gut microbiome on immune responses and the activity of AB4. In parallel, adoptive transfer of CD4[Formula: see text]CD62L[Formula: see text] T cells into Rag1-deficient (Rag1-/-) mice was used to elucidate the alterations in the gut microbiota associated with immune-mediated colitis as well as the modulation by AB4. qPCR, ELISA and western blotting were used to determine the inflammatory responses of mice with colitis, while immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry were employed to determine the CD4[Formula: see text] T cell function and the underlying mechanism. Metagenomic sequencing analysis was used to detect changes in the intestinal microbiota. The depletion of the gut microbiota attenuated disease severity and immune responses in mice with DSS-induced acute and chronic colitis. Notably, the inhibitory effects of orally administered AB4 on colitis progression and immune responses were abrogated. In addition, colitis induced by adoptive transfer of CD4[Formula: see text]CD62L[Formula: see text] T cells into Rag1-/- mice was accompanied by CD4[Formula: see text] T cell engraftment and alterations in gut microbiota. Remarkably, all these pathological changes were significantly attenuated by AB4. Crucially, we found that AB4 suppresses the proliferation, migration, and differentiation of CD4[Formula: see text] T cells, which provides a mechanistic basis for its immunosuppressive effects. Collectively, these findings indicate that the gut microbiota and the immune system, particularly CD4[Formula: see text] T cells, interact with each other in the initiation of colitis. We show that, by targeting this gut microbiota-immune interplay, AB4 is a promising therapeutic strategy for UC.


Deng LR, Zhong YM, Zhu SF, Wu ZY, Chen FJ, Huang CY, Wu QY, Tomlinson B, Tan HE, Li YH


DOI: 10.1142/S0192415X26500849  |  View on PubMed →





Flurbiprofen for Inflammatory Bowel Disease: A Review of Colon-Targeted Formulations.  Recent advances in drug delivery and formulation  |  2026-10-07



Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis are both classified as forms of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD). Strategies that reduce overall systemic exposure while delivering antiinflammatory drug directly to the inflamed colon are necessary for treating IBD. Flurbiprofen is an effective Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drug (NSAID) with potential utility in IBD because it inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 and cyclooxygenase-2, thereby reducing the synthesis of proinflammatory prostaglandins. However, its clinical use for IBD may be limited by gastrointestinal toxicity and the inadequate delivery of conventional oral formulations to the inflamed colonic mucosa. These limitations may result in insufficient drug concentrations at the target site while increasing systemic exposure and the risk of adverse effects. Consequently, colon-targeted flurbiprofen delivery systems are being explored to enhance local therapeutic efficacy and minimize gastrointestinal and systemic toxicity. The current status of colon-targeted drug delivery has improved recently. Flurbiprofen may be locally delivered using techniques such as pH-sensitive coatings, timed release systems, hydrogels, polysaccharide-based matrices, nanoparticles, and microbially triggered platforms. The improvement in both therapeutic efficacy and drug safety in the management of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) with flurbiprofen will depend on integrating preclinical and clinical evidence. Key considerations include current formulation approaches, colon-targeting strategies, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic variables, interspecies differences in intestinal microbiota, stability concerns, and the challenges of translating preclinical findings to humans. Future research should focus on customized delivery systems and hybrid nanocarriers for targeted flurbiprofen delivery, thereby enhancing therapeutic efficacy while minimizing systemic adverse effects.


Chaurasia AK, Tiwari RK, Verma S, Sharma AK


DOI: 10.2174/0126673878478166260924052533  |  View on PubMed →





Eicosapentaenoic Acid-Acylated Astaxanthin Ameliorates DSS-Induced Chronic-Like Relapsing Colitis Associated With Gut Microbiota and Bile Acid Metabolism.  Molecular nutrition & food research  |  2026-10



The role of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) in improving ulcerative colitis (UC) has been extensively studied. EPA-acylated astaxanthin (EA), a novel fish oil, has unclear effects on UC. This study constructed a DSS-induced chronic-like relapsing colitis model in mice induced by 2% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) and primarily concentrated on the changes in gut microbiota and intestinal bile acids (BA) to investigate the anti-UC mechanisms of EA. The results indicated that EA effectively upregulated the expressions of tight junction proteins, ZO-1 and Occludin, while restraining the triggering of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Additionally, EA treatment increased the diversity of the gut microbiota and increased the proportion of Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, and Bifidobacterium, while decreasing the proportion of Bacteroidota, Proteobacteria, and Enterobacteriaceae, which are related to BA metabolism. The metabolomic analysis of BA indicated that EA elevated the concentrations of secondary BA, such as LCA, UDCA, and TUDCA, while decreasing primary BA, such as CA, CDCA, and β-MCA, thereby activating the intestinal ASBT/FXR/TGR5 pathway. In conclusion, EA alleviated DSS-induced colitis, and this protective effect was associated with the modulation of gut microbiota and BA metabolism. The present results laid the foundation for EA as a prospective functional component for UC.


He S, Li X, Zhou M, Jing B, Xia C, Duan J, Li H, Che H


DOI: 10.1002/mnfr.70598  |  View on PubMed →





T-cadherin as a potential novel regulator of intestinal inflammation and fibrosis.Review  Frontiers in physiology  |  2026-09-29



T-cadherin (T-cad) is a non-canonical member of the cadherin superfamily with a distinguished structure of its glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor instead of transmembrane and cytoplasmic domains. This lends unique properties to and equips T-cad with dynamic mobility within the plasma membrane and extensive lateral interactions with signaling partners. Beyond its role as an adhesion molecule forming homophilic interactions, T-cad functions as a receptor for adiponectin and low-density lipoprotein (LDL), therefore playing an important role in regulating cellular processes such as proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These properties underscore its critical involvement in physiological and pathological processes, including central nervous system development, cancer progression, and cardiovascular disease. However, the role of T-cad in intestinal inflammation, injury, and fibrosis remains underexplored. This review highlights the structural and functional characteristics of T-cad, its binding partners, its expression and functions in various types of cells, tissues and organs, and its roles in health and disease. This review also speculates on its potential involvement in intestinal inflammation, particularly in stricturing Crohn’s disease.


Wang Y, Prasad A, Liu W, Chandra J, Zafar A, Naydenov NG, Mukherjee PK, Ivanov AI, Rieder F


DOI: 10.3389/fphys.2026.1946754  |  View on PubMed →





Research progress on intestinal probiotics-mediated protection of the intestinal mucosal barrier in ulcerative colitis.Review  Frontiers in immunology  |  2026-09-28



Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a major subtype of inflammatory bowel disease characterized by a chronic, relapsing course. Its pathogenesis involves complex interactions among gut microbial dysbiosis, epithelial barrier disruption, dysregulated immune responses, and oxidative stress. Impairment of the intestinal mucosal barrier facilitates the translocation of luminal antigens, bacteria, and microbial metabolites into the mucosa, thereby aggravating local inflammation. Probiotics may help maintain barrier homeostasis by reshaping the gut microbial community, reinforcing epithelial and mucus barriers, modulating mucosal immunity, and reducing oxidative injury. Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease with a complex and incompletely understood pathogenesis. This study aimed to prioritize candidate genes associated with UC and characterize their potential genetic and immune-related molecular context using an integrative transcriptomic and genetic framework. Bulk transcriptomic analysis was first performed using the discovery cohort GSE87466. After duplicated gene symbols were collapsed by mean expression, differential expression analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) were conducted to identify UC-related candidate genes. Candidate genes for downstream analyses were defined by the overlap between differentially expressed genes and genes within selected WGCNA core modules. An expression quantitative trait locus-based summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) framework integrating UC genome-wide association study data with blood-derived eQTL data was subsequently applied to prioritize putative gene-disease associations. Functional enrichment analysis, CIBERSORT-based immune infiltration analysis, single-gene gene set enrichment analysis, and single-cell RNA sequencing analyses were performed to characterize the biological context of the prioritized genes. Three independent transcriptomic cohorts were used for external validation, and a small DSS-induced colitis mouse experiment was used for exploratory experimental assessment. eQTL-based SMR analysis identified IRF1 and JAK2 as candidate genes associated with UC susceptibility. IRF1 was prioritized for downstream characterization based on convergent evidence from transcriptomic, immune, single-cell, and experimental analyses. IRF1 expression was associated with multiple CIBERSORT-inferred immune-cell proportions, including positive correlations with M1 macrophages, neutrophils, activated dendritic cells, and T follicular helper cells, and negative correlations with M2 macrophages and activated natural killer cells. Higher IRF1 expression was associated with interferon, NF-κB, and IL-6/JAK/STAT3 signaling pathways. Single-cell analysis showed IRF1 expression across myeloid cells, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and epithelial cells. DSS-treated mice showed descriptively higher colonic IRF1 protein expression, providing preliminary experimental support consistent with human transcriptomic findings. IRF1 was prioritized as a candidate gene associated with UC and was linked to interferon-related inflammatory pathways and altered immune-cell profiles. These findings provide an integrated framework for further investigation of the potential role of IRF1 in UC. [The Great Imposter: Three Cases of Inflammatory Bowel Disease Associated with Innate Immune Defects].Case report  Acta gastroenterologica Latinoamericana  |  2026-09-30



Pediatric inflammatory bowel disease associated with inborn errors of immunity represents a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge, particularly in cases of early-onset, severe disease, extraintestinal manifestations, or refractoriness to treatment. We present three pediatric cases with an aggressive clinical course, multisystemic involvement, and an inadequate response to multiple therapeutic lines of therapy, in whom the persistent presence of warning signs prompted genetic testing. In one of these patients, exome sequencing identified a pathogenic variant in FOXP3, confirming the diagnosis of IPEX syndrome. In the other two patients, who were siblings, an alteration in XIAP was identified, consistent with a diagnosis of X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome type 2. In the index patient with XIAP deficiency, the initial exome sequencing did not identify any causative variants. Subsequently, genome sequencing established the molecular diagnosis, which subsequently led to the cascade diagnosis of his sibling. These cases highlight the importance of early recognition of phenotypes suggestive of monogenic disease, maintaining diagnostic suspicion despite initially negative genetic test results, and conducting a timely multidisciplinary evaluation. Identification of an underlying inborn error of immunity can substantially modify the therapeutic approach, allow for the consideration of potentially curative options such as hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and facilitate family genetic counseling. La enfermedad inflamatoria intestinal pediátrica asociada a errores innatos de la inmunidad representa un desafío diagnóstico y terapéutico, en especial en los casos de inicio temprano, enfermedad grave, manifestaciones extraintestinales o refractariedad al tratamiento. Presentamos tres casos pediátricos con un curso clínico agresivo, compromiso multisistémico y respuesta insuficiente a múltiples líneas terapéuticas, en quienes la presencia persistente de señales de alarma motivó la realización de estudios genéticos. En uno de ellos, la secuenciación del exoma identificó una variante patogénica en FOXP3, confirmando el diagnóstico de síndrome IPEX. En los otros dos pacientes, hermanos entre sí, se identificó una alteración en XIAP compatible con diagnóstico de síndrome linfoproliferativo ligado al X tipo 2. En el paciente índice con deficiencia de XIAP, el exoma inicial no identificó variantes causales. Posteriormente, la secuenciación del genoma permitió establecer el diagnóstico molecular, lo que condujo al diagnóstico familiar en cascada de su hermano. Estos casos resaltan la importancia de reconocer tempranamente los fenotipos sugestivos de enfermedad monogénica, mantener la sospecha diagnóstica ante estudios genéticos iniciales negativos y realizar una evaluación multidisciplinaria oportuna. La identificación de un error innato de la inmunidad subyacente puede modificar sustancialmente el abordaje terapéutico, permitir la consideración de opciones potencialmente curativas como el trasplante de progenitores hematopoyéticos y facilitar el asesoramiento genético familiar.

Severe malnutrition and persistent myopenia despite weight recovery in newly diagnosed stricturing Crohn’s disease: A case report.  Nutrition in clinical practice : official publication of the American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition  |  2026-10-14



Protein-energy malnutrition is a common complication in Crohn’s disease (CD). In addition to weight loss, patients may develop significant alterations in body composition, including skeletal muscle depletion, which can negatively affect clinical outcomes and quality of life. Herein, we report on a patient with newly diagnosed CD who presented with severe malnutrition and myopenia, which persisted despite improvements in nutritional intake and body weight. A 27-year-old woman was admitted with abdominal pain, decreased appetite, nausea, vomiting, and progressive weight loss (10 kg, 22% of her usual body weight). Based on clinical presentation, family history, and magnetic resonance enterography findings, stricturing CD was diagnosed. Nutritional assessment revealed severe malnutrition (body weight, 31 kg; body mass index, 12.26 kg/m2; phase angle, 4.4°, intracellular-to-extracellular mass ratio, 0.75). Computed tomography-based body composition analysis demonstrated marked skeletal muscle depletion (skeletal muscle index, 27.5 cm2/m2), confirming myopenia. The patient was treated with corticosteroids, infliximab, azathioprine, and multidisciplinary nutritional management. After 12 months of follow-up, she achieved clinical remission and gained approximately 25% of her initial body weight. Despite significant weight recovery and improved dietary intake, computed tomography (CT) revealed low skeletal muscle mass and increased visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue, indicating persistent myopenia. This case highlights the importance of comprehensive body composition assessments in CD. Clinical remission and weight gain may not accurately reflect recovery of skeletal muscle mass. Early nutritional evaluation and longitudinal body composition monitoring may be helpful in the management of patients with CD to identify persistent muscle depletion and optimize long-term outcomes.

Capsaicin, the pungent vanilloid of chili pepper, is a widely consumed dietary constituent that exerts pleiotropic actions on physiological and pathophysiological processes, including anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antiproliferative, metabolic and cardioprotective effects. Capsaicin is a small, highly lipophilic molecule that is not appreciably hydrolyzed by digestive enzymes in the gut lumen; it is absorbed across the gastrointestinal epithelium largely in its intact form, mainly by passive diffusion, and enters the portal circulation, where it undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism in the intestinal epithelium and liver before reaching the systemic circulation. Its principal molecular target, transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1), is upregulated in the inflamed colonic mucosa of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a chronic relapsing disorder in which current therapies remain limited by incomplete efficacy, loss of response and cumulative toxicity. Because capsaicin activates TRPV1 on capsaicin-sensitive sensory neurons and can thereby evoke burning pain and neurogenic inflammation, its potential relevance to IBD was long overlooked. In recent years, however, a growing body of preclinical evidence has shown that capsaicin can attenuate experimental colitis through multiple pathways, including anti-inflammatory action, mucosal protection, microbiota regulation and microcirculation regulation, whereas higher doses, certain routes of administration and an already-inflamed mucosa favour adverse effects-consistent with the bell-shaped dose-response relationship reported for capsaicin. This review summarizes the evidence for the protective effects of capsaicin in IBD, outlines its gastrointestinal adverse effects and the TRPV1-dependent mechanisms that underlie them, and discusses how dose, route, duration of exposure and disease stage determine whether capsaicin acts as friend or foe.

Biotherapeutics are required to achieve high remission rates in patients with severe ulcerative colitis (UC); however, adverse effects, complex dosing regimens, administration routes, and low patient compliance limit their widespread clinical use. Given the localized nature of UC, this study aimed to develop localized delivery strategies for infliximab (IFX), an anti-tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) monoclonal antibody recommended for moderately-to-severely active UC. Exploiting the intrinsic biocompatibility, mucoadhesion, and protein-entrapment capacity of lipid mesophases (LMPs), IFX was encapsulated within the gel matrix, providing protection against enzymatic and environmental degradation. IFX-LMPs were designed for targeted delivery to inflamed colonic tissues via rectal or oral administration, with oral dosage forms manufactured either by 3D printing or by encapsulation into enteric capsules. A comprehensive physicochemical characterization was performed to elucidate mesophase self-assembly and its relationship with IFX release profiles in biorelevant fluids. The rectal gel demonstrated strong mucoadhesion, while LMP-loaded enteric capsules enabled effective colon targeting. In a prophylactic treatment setting, LMP-based formulations significantly attenuated disease progression and the development of severe inflammation compared with subcutaneous IFX. Overall, this study establishes a biocompatible delivery platform that enables colon-targeted IFX release, representing a promising therapeutic strategy for UC using biotherapeutics.

Biologics improve outcomes in inflammatory bowel disease, but high costs restrict access and strain healthcare resources. Biosimilars lower costs, expand access, and support sustainable IBD care. Provide clear, evidence-based answers on biosimilar use in IBD across clinical, therapeutic, and economic domains to guide safe implementation and informed decision-making. GEDIIB conducted a PICO-structured systematic review across multiple databases and trial registries. We extracted clinically relevant outcomes and performed systematic review. We assessed risk of bias with RoB 2.0 and ROBINS-I and graded certainty using GRADE. A structured Delphi process with two voting rounds and external validation finalized recommendations, with consensus predefined at 85 percent or higher. Anti-TNF biosimilars and originator biologics have similar efficacy, safety, immunogenicity, treatment persistence, and mucosal healing in biologic-naive patients and after switching, with no clinically meaningful differences in adverse events, loss of response, or discontinuation. Data on multiple switches do not indicate harm, though evidence remains limited. Pediatric studies suggest similar profiles, with lower precision. Economic evaluations show substantial cost savings and improved access, supporting the sustainability of the health system. Biosimilars represent a viable, safe, and cost-effective option for IBD management. We recommend structured switching strategies, clear communication with patients, and continuous clinical monitoring. Additional robust studies should strengthen evidence in specific populations and clinical scenarios. Os medicamentos biológicos melhoraram significativamente os desfechos clínicos na doença inflamatória intestinal (DII); entretanto, seus elevados custos limitam o acesso ao tratamento e impõem um impacto considerável aos sistemas de saúde. Os biossimilares reduzem custos, ampliam o acesso aos tratamentos e contribuem para a sustentabilidade da assistência aos pacientes com DII. Fornecer respostas claras e baseadas em evidências sobre o uso de biossimilares na DII, abrangendo aspectos clínicos, terapêuticos e econômicos, a fim de orientar sua implementação segura e subsidiar a tomada de decisões informadas. A Organização Brasileira de Crohn e Colite (GEDIIB) conduziu uma revisão sistemática estruturada segundo a metodologia PICO, abrangendo múltiplas bases de dados e registros de ensaios clínicos. Foram extraídos desfechos clinicamente relevantes e realizada uma revisão sistemática. O risco de viés foi avaliado por meio das ferramentas RoB 2.0 e ROBINS-I, e a certeza da evidência foi classificada utilizando a metodologia GRADE. As recomendações foram elaboradas e validadas por meio de um processo Delphi estruturado, composto por duas rodadas de votação e de validação externa, tendo como consenso a concordância igual ou superior a 85%. Os biossimilares anti-TNF e os biológicos originadores apresentam eficácia, segurança, imunogenicidade, persistência terapêutica e cicatrização mucosa semelhantes, tanto em pacientes virgens de tratamento biológico quanto após a troca do medicamento originador para o biossimilar. Não foram observadas diferenças clinicamente relevantes na ocorrência de eventos adversos, na perda de resposta ou na descontinuação do tratamento. Os dados disponíveis sobre múltiplas trocas não sugerem prejuízo clínico, embora as evidências permaneçam limitadas. Estudos pediátricos apontam perfis comparáveis de eficácia e segurança, porém com menor precisão das estimativas. Avaliações econômicas demonstram uma economia substancial de recursos e a ampliação do acesso ao tratamento, favorecendo a sustentabilidade dos sistemas de saúde. Os biossimilares representam uma alternativa viável, segura e custo-efetiva para o manejo da DII. Recomenda-se a adoção de estratégias estruturadas de troca terapêutica, de comunicação clara com os pacientes e de monitoramento clínico contínuo. Estudos adicionais, metodologicamente robustos, são necessários para fortalecer as evidências em populações específicas e em cenários clínicos particulares.

Intestinal T-cell migration: unraveling mechanisms and therapeutic implications.Review  Journal of advanced research  |  2026-10-10



Intestinal T-cell migration links mucosal immunity with systemic immune homeostasis and contributes to immune surveillance, barrier defense, and peripheral tissue inflammation. Advances in single-cell omics, spatial analysis, and intravital imaging are reshaping our understanding of its subset specificity and tissue selectivity. This review summarizes the molecular mechanisms, microenvironmental regulation, pathological significance along the gut-organ axes, and related therapeutic strategies of intestinal T-cell migration, with a particular focus on how migratory imbalance contributes to intestinal and extraintestinal immune-mediated diseases. Intestinal T-cell migration is jointly driven by gut imprinting, S1P-S1PR-mediated egress, chemokine-guided trafficking, integrin-dependent adhesion, and cytoskeletal remodeling, and is further regulated by metabolic, epigenetic, and microbial signals. This process is highly dependent on T-cell subset and tissue context: it promotes effector T-cell recruitment and inflammatory amplification in inflammatory bowel disease, manifests as restricted antitumor T-cell infiltration in colorectal cancer, and may contribute to distant tissue injury through the gut-organ axes. Existing S1PR modulators, integrin antagonists, and chemokine-targeted strategies have demonstrated the therapeutic tractability of migratory pathways; however, pathway redundancy, tissue heterogeneity, and impairment of protective immunity continue to limit their application. Future strategies should move beyond broad suppression of migration toward subset-, tissue-, and disease stage-specific precision modulation, combined with microbiota-based interventions and biomarker-guided stratification to improve therapeutic efficacy.

Smart Oral Capsule with a Closed-Loop Sense-Decide-Act Strategy for Colitis Therapy.  ACS sensors  |  2026-10-14



Current treatments for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) lack real-time inflammatory monitoring and lesion-specific drug delivery, resulting in poor efficacy and systemic toxicity. To address this, we present a smart oral capsule that operates a closed-loop “sense-decide-act” strategy entirely autonomously-sensing and drug release are driven by changes in the digestive tract environment without any external intervention. The capsule features a dual-layer shell sequentially responsive to pH and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), enabling colon-targeted delivery and inflammation-specific activation. An integrated multimodal sensor wirelessly tracks colonic TNF-α (>5 ng mL-1), pH (>7.0), and Na+ (>100 mM). The encapsulated budesonide nanoparticles (Bud@PEG-SS-NPs) release the drug specifically in reactive oxygen species (ROS)-rich microenvironments and show superior anti-inflammatory efficacy in both lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced cellular models and dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse colitis. In live rats, the capsule achieved on-demand drug release in response to elevated local TNF-α levels, and a single intervention significantly alleviated inflammation. This work establishes a new paradigm for personalized, adaptive IBD therapy and provides a versatile platform for closed-loop management of other gastrointestinal diseases.

Reflecting on Quality-of-Care Delivery in Inflammatory Bowel Disease Pregnancy: The (Pause and Reflect) PAUSA Study.  Digestive diseases and sciences  |  2026-10-07



Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) have been associated with adverse outcomes during pregnancy, with guidelines developed to inform clinical practice. This study reviewed adherence to guidelines amongst different healthcare providers caring for individuals with IBD during pregnancy. A retrospective multi-centre study of individuals with IBD who received antenatal IBD care at three Australian tertiary units from 2023 to 2025 was undertaken. Clinical documentation for each pregnancy was reviewed against nine process indicators derived from the European Crohn’s and Colitis Guidelines on Sexuality, Fertility, Pregnancy and Lactation [1]. The primary outcome was the proportion of process indicators followed by speciality per pregnancy. Forty-three pregnancies amongst 43 individuals were included; 19 (44.2%) had ulcerative colitis. Twenty-six pregnancies (60.5%) were to individuals on biologic therapy for IBD at time of conception. Gastroenterologists met a median 6/9 (67%) process indicators, Obstetrics/Maternofetal Medicine specialists met a median 3/9 (33%) process indicators, and Other Specialists (combined) met a median 1/9 (11%) process indicators per pregnancy. The number of clinic visits and proportion of process indicators followed correlated positively. Adherence to preconception counselling, mental health assessment, and venous thromboembolism risk assessment was particularly poor, completed by Gastroenterology in 39.5, 34.9 and 4.7% of cases, respectively, compared to 4.7, 25.6 and 46.5% of cases by obstetric care providers. Uptake of guideline recommendations for antenatal IBD management was variable between different speciality providers in this study of patients with moderate-to-severe IBD. Uptake of recommendations may be improved by increasing access to multidisciplinary care and frequent clinical contact. Whether improvements in adherence with process indicators translates to improved clinical outcomes warrants further evaluation in IBD pregnancy.
